# Evaluating and Improving Agentic Systems {#evaluating-agentic-systems}

An agentic system has many parts: prompts, models, retrievers, tools, and the
code that connects them. When it does not work well enough, which is most of
the time during development, almost any part could be to blame. Teams that
improve quickly differ from teams that stall mainly in how they decide **what
to work on next**. In Andrew Ng's experience, a disciplined process of
evaluation and error analysis is one of the strongest predictors of how
effective a team will be.

This chapter covers that process:

1. build a quick prototype and look at its outputs;
2. turn recurring problems into **end-to-end evals**;
3. read **traces** and run **error analysis** to find the component
   responsible;
4. build **component-level evals** to improve that component efficiently; and
5. once quality is good enough, optimize **cost and latency**.

The reflection chapter (Section \@ref(measuring-whether-reflection-helps))
used a small version of this process to decide whether a reflection step was
worth keeping. Here it becomes a general method.

## Build first, then look

It is hard to predict where an agentic system will fail. Weeks of up-front
design often guess wrong. The more productive approach is to **build a quick,
safe prototype**, one that does not leak data or take irreversible actions,
and then **read its outputs**.

Take 10 to 20 realistic inputs, run them, and note what is wrong with each
output in a spreadsheet. Patterns appear quickly:

- An **invoice-processing** workflow keeps extracting the *issue* date when the
  task needs the *due* date.
- An **ad-copy** assistant writes good headlines, but many exceed the
  30-character headline limit of Google search ads.
- A **campaign-insights** agent writes fluent summaries but sometimes misses
  the point a senior analyst would lead with, such as a budget overspend.

Each observation leads to one of two actions. If the fix is obvious, such as a
missing instruction, **just fix it**. If improving it will take sustained
iteration, **build an eval** for that problem so you can measure progress.

Looking at outputs also tells you *what* to evaluate. You cannot write a good
rubric before seeing how the system fails. @shankar2024validators call this
**criteria drift**: people need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs
is how they discover their criteria. Expect your evals to change as you learn.

> **In short.**
>
> - You cannot predict the failures; build a safe prototype and read 10–20
>   outputs.
> - Fix obvious problems directly; build an eval for anything that needs
>   sustained work.
> - Criteria come from reading outputs, so expect them to change.

## End-to-end evals

An **end-to-end eval** measures the final output for a given input, treating
the whole system as one unit. End-to-end evals differ along two axes:

- **Who grades:** code (objective checks) or an LLM judge (subjective
  judgments).
- **What the output is compared with:** a **per-example reference** (each
  input has its own correct answer or key points) or a **shared criterion**
  (the same rule applies to every example).

| | **Per-example reference** | **Shared criterion** |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Code grades** | Invoice due date matches the labeled date | Headline is at most 30 characters; output is valid JSON; no competitor names |
| **LLM judge grades** | Report mentions the 3–5 key points an expert listed for this question | Chart passes a rubric (title, axis labels, chart type); reply has a professional tone |

### Code-graded evals

Prefer code whenever the criterion is objective. It is cheap, fast, and
deterministic. Make outputs easy to check: if the prompt tells the model to
write dates as `YYYY-MM-DD`, a few lines of code can grade them.

```python
import re

def due_date_correct(output: str, label: str) -> bool:
    """Compare the first ISO date in the model output with the labeled due date."""
    match = re.search(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", output)
    return bool(match) and match.group() == label

accuracy = sum(due_date_correct(o, y) for o, y in zip(outputs, labels)) / len(labels)
```

For the ad-copy example there is no per-example label; the check is simply
`len(headline) <= 30` for every output.

### LLM-judged evals

When the criterion needs reading comprehension, use an LLM judge. Suppose
that for each question in the campaign-insights eval set, an analyst has
written the three to five points a good answer must cover. Key points can be
phrased in many ways, so string matching fails, but a judge can count them:

```text
You are grading a campaign-performance summary.

<question>{question}</question>
<key_points>{expert_key_points}</key_points>
<summary>{agent_output}</summary>

For each key point, decide whether the summary states it clearly
(paraphrase is fine). Return JSON:
{"explanation": "<one line per key point>", "points_covered": <integer>}
```

Asking for the explanation **before** the score makes the judge commit to its
reasoning first, and the explanation is what you read when the score looks
wrong.

### Making LLM judges trustworthy

LLM judges have known biases, including position bias, a preference for longer
answers, and a preference for their own outputs [@zheng2023judge]. The
fine-tuning chapter introduced them (Section \@ref(beyond-overlap-metrics)),
and the reflection
chapter showed how position bias can reverse direction. Practical defenses:

- **Grade one output at a time against a rubric** of specific yes/no
  criteria, instead of asking which of two outputs is better.
- **Give the judge references** (key points, a correct answer, the source
  document) whenever you have them.
- **If you must compare pairs, evaluate both orders** and count only
  consistent verdicts.
- **Use a different model family as judge** from the one that generated the
  outputs, to reduce self-preference.
- **Validate the judge against human labels.** Have a person grade 50 to 100
  examples and measure agreement with the judge. Raw agreement can look high
  when most outputs pass, so also report **Cohen's kappa**, which corrects for
  agreement expected by chance [@cohen1960kappa]. Re-check whenever the judge
  prompt or model changes.

**Example: why raw agreement misleads.** A person and a judge each grade 100
replies. Each passes 90 of them, and they agree on 90 (85 both pass, 5 both
fail). Raw agreement is 90%, which sounds excellent. But two graders who pass
90% of replies at random would agree $0.9 \times 0.9 + 0.1 \times 0.1 = 82\%$
of the time. Kappa measures agreement beyond that baseline:

$$
\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e} = \frac{0.90 - 0.82}{1 - 0.82} \approx 0.44
$$

That is only moderate agreement. The judge agrees with the person mostly
because almost everything passes. It catches only half of the 10 failures
the person found, and those failures are what the eval exists to find.

### Start small, then grow the set

Teams sometimes delay evals because they imagine a multi-week project. A
first eval with 10 to 20 examples and a simple metric is far better than
none. Use it **alongside** reading outputs, not instead of it. As the eval
grows and proves reliable, you can trust the metric more and read fewer
outputs after each change.

Improve the eval as you go:

- **When the metric disagrees with your judgment**, such as when you are sure
  a change helped but the score did not move, treat that as a bug in the eval.
  Add examples or change how outputs are graded.
- **Add examples from real failures**, edge cases, and inputs where the system
  falls short of an expert. For tasks that people already do, places where the
  system is worse than a skilled human are the best guide to what to improve.
- **Keep a held-out set.** If you tune prompts against the same 20 examples
  for weeks, you will overfit to them, just as with training data in machine
  learning. Check the final configuration on examples you did not tune on.

### How much should you trust a score?

An eval score is an estimate from a sample, so it has sampling error. For an
accuracy $\hat p$ measured on $n$ independent examples, the standard error is
$\sqrt{\hat p (1 - \hat p) / n}$. At $\hat p = 0.8$:

| Examples ($n$) | Standard error | Approximate 95% interval |
|---:|---:|:--|
| 20 | 8.9 points | 80% ± 17.5 points |
| 100 | 4.0 points | 80% ± 7.8 points |
| 400 | 2.0 points | 80% ± 3.9 points |

A 20-example eval is good for catching large regressions and for guiding early
work. It cannot distinguish 80% from 85%. @miller2024errorbars sets out a
statistical approach to model evals that applies directly here:

- **Report standard errors** with every score.
- **Use clustered standard errors** when examples come in related groups,
  such as several questions about the same campaign.
- **Analyze paired differences** when comparing two systems on the same
  examples. The question-level comparison is far more precise than comparing
  two overall accuracies (McNemar's test is the binary case).
- **Reduce variance by resampling.** Run each example several times when
  outputs are non-deterministic and average the results. For agents that users
  run repeatedly, also report how often *all* of $k$ runs succeed (pass^k,
  Section \@ref(evaluation-is-a-harness-too)).
- **Do a power analysis** before concluding that a change made no difference.
  The eval may simply be too small to detect it.

> **In short.**
>
> - End-to-end evals have two axes: code or LLM judge, per-example reference
>   or shared criterion. Use code whenever the criterion is objective.
> - Trust a judge only after checking it against human labels, with kappa,
>   not just raw agreement.
> - Start with 10–20 examples, grow from real failures, keep a held-out set,
>   and report error bars.

## Traces and spans

End-to-end evals tell you *that* something is wrong, not *where*. For that,
you need the **trace**: the record of everything the system did for one
input. The terms come from software observability. In OpenTelemetry, a
**trace** is the path of one request through an application, and a **span**
is one unit of work within it, with its own timing and attributes
[@otel2024traces]. In an agentic system, each LLM call, tool call, or
retrieval step is a span.

For each span, log at least:

- its inputs and outputs (the full prompt and completion for LLM calls);
- the model, prompt version, and parameters;
- tool names, arguments, results, and errors;
- tokens, latency, and cost.

A trace for one run of the campaign-insights agent might look like this
(simplified):

```text
trace  q-0117  "Why did CPA rise on Search last week?"        total 27.4 s  $0.07
├─ span interpret_question  llm  2.1 s   in 1,200 tok  out 150 tok
│    output: {"channel": "Search", "metric": "CPA", "period": "2026-10-12..18"}
├─ span write_sql           llm  3.8 s   in 2,900 tok  out 240 tok
│    output: SELECT ... WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2026-10-12' AND '2026-10-18'
├─ span run_query           tool 9.3 s   rows 14
└─ span write_narrative     llm 12.2 s   in 6,400 tok  out 610 tok
     output: "CPA on Search rose 18%, driven by ..."
```

Reading it, an analyst would spot that the SQL filters on `order_date` when
the metric needs the conversion date. Nothing in the final narrative reveals
that; only the trace does.

The habit that matters most is simple: **read traces regularly**, not only
when something breaks. Many tools exist to collect and browse traces. On
Databricks, for example, MLflow Tracing records agent runs and connects to
MLflow's evaluation tooling (Chapter \@ref(context-harness-engineering)).

> **In short.**
>
> - A trace is the record of one run; a span is one step in it.
> - Log inputs, outputs, versions, tool calls, tokens, latency, and cost for
>   every span.
> - Read traces regularly; they show failures the final output hides.

## Error analysis {#agentic-error-analysis}

**Error analysis** is the systematic reading of traces for examples where the
system failed, in order to find which component is responsible.

Consider a campaign-insights agent with four steps: **interpret** the
question, **write SQL**, **run the query** on the warehouse, and **write the
narrative**. The end-to-end eval shows that summaries often miss key points.
Any step could be the cause. The question might be misread, the SQL might
filter the wrong dates, the warehouse might hold stale data, or the writer
might ignore a number it was given. Picking a component by gut feeling
sometimes works. It also sometimes leads to months of work on a part that was
never the problem.

### The procedure

1. **Collect failures.** Set aside the examples the system got right. Gather
   10 to 100 examples where the final output was unsatisfactory.
2. **Walk each trace step by step.** For each component, ask: *given the
   input this component received*, is its output clearly worse than what a
   skilled person would produce?
3. **Blame a component only for its own work.** If the query returned stale
   data, the writer cannot be faulted for reporting it. The writer did as well
   as anyone could with what it was given.
4. **Record the judgment in a spreadsheet**, one row per failed example and
   one column per component, with a short note.
5. **Count.** For each component, compute the share of failed examples in
   which it erred.

An illustrative result for 20 failed examples:

| Example | Interpret question | Write SQL | Warehouse data | Write narrative | Note |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--|
| 1 | | ✗ | | | Filtered on order date instead of conversion date |
| 2 | | ✗ | | ✗ | Wrong join; summary also buried the main result |
| 3 | | | ✗ | | Yesterday's spend not loaded |
| … | | | | | |
| **Share of failures** | **10%** | **60%** | **10%** | **35%** | |

The shares add up to more than 100% because one example can have errors in
several components.

### From counts to priorities

The counts are evidence, not a decision. Prioritize a component when:

- it causes a **large share** of failures;
- you have **concrete ideas** for improving it; and
- those ideas are **affordable** in time and cost.

Here, SQL generation is the clear first target, and the narrative step comes
second. Remember that the shares are fractions of *failures*. If 30% of
outputs fail overall and SQL errors appear in 60% of those, eliminating SQL
errors entirely would cut the failure rate by at most 18 percentage points.
That is an upper bound, because some of those examples also have other
errors. A related check from classic machine learning practice is **ceiling
analysis**: substitute a correct output for one component (for example,
hand-written SQL) and measure how much the end-to-end score rises. That tells
you how much fixing the component could ever be worth.

The same procedure applies to simpler workflows. For the invoice workflow,
the question is whether the PDF-to-text step garbled the dates (so that even
a person could not read them from its output) or whether the LLM picked the
wrong date from clean text. If the LLM step accounts for most errors, weeks
spent tuning the PDF converter would be wasted. In a research agent, the
usual culprit is search: when the sources are poor, the writing step cannot
recover, and a component eval on search (Section
\@ref(component-level-evals)) is the right next step.

**Starting the categories.** If you do not yet know which failure types to
count, write a free-text note for each failed example first. Then group the
notes into categories and count those. The categories usually map onto
components or onto specific behaviors, such as "ignored date filter" or
"invented a metric", that can each become an eval.

> **In short.**
>
> - Read the traces of failed examples and blame each component only for its
>   own output, given its input.
> - Count the share of failures per component; the shares can sum past 100%.
> - Prioritize components that cause many failures and that you know how to
>   improve. Ceiling analysis bounds the gain.

## Component-level evals

Once error analysis has pointed to a component, improving it by rerunning the
full system after every change is slow and expensive. It is also noisy:
randomness in the other components can hide a small real improvement. A
**component-level eval** measures that one component directly.

**Example: retrieval or web search.** For a set of queries, have an expert
list the sources a good search should find. Then score each configuration on
how well its results match:

- **Precision**: the fraction of returned results that are relevant.
- **Recall**: the fraction of relevant results that were returned.
- **F1**: the harmonic mean of the two, $2PR/(P+R)$.

For one query, suppose the expert lists 5 sources and the search returns 8
results, 3 of which are on the expert's list. Precision is $3/8 = 0.375$,
recall is $3/5 = 0.6$, and F1 is $2 \times 0.375 \times 0.6 / 0.975 \approx
0.46$. Average these over the query set to score a configuration.

Ranked variants such as precision@k and recall@k are standard in information
retrieval [@manning2008ir]. With this eval you can quickly compare search
providers, the number of results, date ranges, or chunking strategies.

**Example: SQL generation.** Compare the *result* of the generated query with
the result of a reference query, not the SQL text. Many different queries are
correct.

**Example: tool use.** Measure tool-selection and argument accuracy on
labeled requests (Section \@ref(evaluating-tool-use)).

Component evals also let a team own one clear metric without running the
whole system. They have one danger: a component metric can improve while the
end-to-end result does not, because the metric does not capture what
downstream steps need. **Always confirm with the end-to-end eval** before
declaring a component improvement done.

> **In short.**
>
> - A component eval measures one step directly: faster, cheaper, and less
>   noisy than rerunning the whole system.
> - Retrieval: precision, recall, F1 against expert-chosen sources. SQL:
>   compare query results, not query text.
> - Confirm every component gain end to end.

## Improving a component

**Non-LLM components** (search engines, retrievers, OCR, classifiers) usually
have settings to tune or alternatives to swap:

- web search: the provider, number of results, date range, domain filters;
- retrieval (Section \@ref(retrieval-augmented-generation-rag)): chunk size,
  embedding model, similarity threshold, number of chunks;
- a detector or classifier: the decision threshold, which trades false
  positives against false negatives.

**LLM components** have a standard ladder of options, roughly from cheapest to
most expensive:

1. **Improve the prompt.** Add explicit instructions, context, and a few
   input–output examples (Chapter \@ref(prompt-anatomy)).
2. **Try a different model.** Use your evals to choose. A multi-provider
   interface makes this cheap to test.
3. **Decompose the step.** A prompt with many instructions may be too much for
   one call. Split it into two or three simpler calls (Chapter
   \@ref(agentic-workflows)), or add a reflection step (Chapter
   \@ref(reflection)).
4. **Fine-tune.** Fine-tuning can add the last few points on a mature system
   with enough labeled data, but it costs the most development time
   (Chapter \@ref(instruction-fine-tuning-and-evaluation)). Try the cheaper
   options first.

### Building intuition about models

Choosing models well is faster when you have a feel for what each one is
good at. Models differ: some are stronger at coding, some at following long
instructions, some at particular domains, and they differ in price and speed.
Smaller models often answer simple factual questions well but follow complex,
multi-part instructions less reliably. Benchmarks of **verifiable
instructions**, such as IFEval's "write more than 400 words" or "mention a
keyword at least three times", measure this ability with code
[@zhou2023ifeval].

Consider redacting personal information from customer-call summaries before
analysis. A capable model removes every name, address, and account number,
and returns exactly the requested format. A weaker model may miss a name,
redact an address only partly, or add a list nobody asked for. You can catch
this with a component eval: label the personal-information spans in 50
summaries and check, in code, that none survive.

Ways to build this intuition:

- **Try new models when they are released**, on a small personal set of
  prompts that you reuse across models.
- **Read other people's prompts**, including those in respected open-source
  projects, to learn what instructions models follow well.
- **Swap models within your own workflows** and compare them with traces and
  evals, noting quality, price, and speed.

> **In short.**
>
> - Non-LLM components: tune settings or swap providers.
> - LLM components, cheapest first: better prompt, different model,
>   decompose or add reflection, fine-tune last.
> - Build model intuition by testing new models on your own small prompt set.

## Cost and latency {#agentic-cost-latency}

Get output quality right first. It is usually the hardest part, and a fast,
cheap system that gives wrong answers has no value. Once quality is
acceptable, and especially once usage grows, cost and latency start to matter.

The method mirrors error analysis: **measure each step**, then optimize the
steps that dominate. Steps are billed in different ways:

- **LLM calls** are billed **per token**, input and output priced separately.
- **External APIs** (search, data providers, PDF conversion) are usually
  billed **per call** or per page.
- **Compute** (a warehouse query, a code sandbox, a self-hosted model) is
  billed by **capacity used**, such as seconds of compute or server hours.

An illustrative breakdown for one run of the campaign-insights agent, with
one extra step that pulls competitor benchmarks from a paid data API. The
dollar figures are made up for the example, not real prices:

| Step | Billing basis | Latency | Cost per run |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| Interpret question (small LLM) | Per token | 2 s | \$0.001 |
| Write SQL (mid-size LLM, schema in prompt) | Per token | 4 s | \$0.010 |
| Run query (warehouse) | Compute time | 9 s | \$0.015 |
| Pull competitor benchmarks (paid data API) | Per call | 3 s | \$0.080 |
| Write narrative (strong LLM, long context) | Per token | 12 s | \$0.060 |
| **Total** | | **30 s** | **\$0.166** |

Two lessons. For **latency**, speeding up the interpretation step barely
matters; the narrative and the query are the targets. As Amdahl's law says,
the overall speed-up is limited by the share of time spent in the part you
improve. For **cost**, the single API call costs more than all three LLM
steps together (\$0.071). Switching to a cheaper model would barely help;
caching benchmark results, or calling the API only when the question needs
it, would. Only measuring each step shows this.

Levers for **latency**:

- run independent steps **in parallel**, such as several searches or fetches;
- use a **smaller or faster model** for a step, if its eval still passes;
- try a **faster serving provider** for the same model;
- **stream** the final output so users see progress; and
- **trim context**, because long prompts take longer to process.

Levers for **cost**:

- a **cheaper model** for steps that do not need the strongest one;
- **prompt caching** for long, repeated prefixes such as instructions and tool
  definitions;
- **batch APIs** for work that does not need an immediate answer;
- **fewer tokens**: shorter prompts, concise tool results, capped loops; and
- **cheaper tools or plans** where per-call API fees dominate.

Measuring often shows that some steps are not worth optimizing at all.

> **In short.**
>
> - Quality first; then measure latency and cost per step and work on the
>   steps that dominate.
> - LLMs bill per token, APIs per call, compute by capacity. A non-LLM step
>   can be the most expensive one.
> - Latency: parallelize, smaller models, faster providers, trimmed context,
>   streaming. Cost: cheaper models, caching, batching, fewer tokens.

## The build–analyze loop

Developing an agentic system alternates between two activities: **building**
(writing code, prompts, and tools) and **analyzing** (reading outputs and
traces, running evals and error analysis). Analysis can feel like it is not
progress, but it is what makes the building effective. Less experienced teams
tend to spend too much time building and too little analyzing.

The analysis becomes more rigorous as the system matures:

| Stage | Analysis |
|:--|:--|
| Prototype | Read final outputs and a few traces; fix obvious problems |
| Early | Small end-to-end evals (10–20 examples) on the problems you found |
| Maturing | Systematic error analysis: count which components cause failures |
| Mature | Component-level evals for the parts you are actively improving; larger, held-out end-to-end evals with error bars |

The process is not linear. You will move back and forth between tuning the
whole system, analyzing errors, and improving single components.

> **Current practice (October 2026).** Many platforms record traces, run
> evals, and track cost: open-source and commercial LLM observability tools,
> MLflow on Databricks, and the providers' own consoles. They save
> engineering time. However, most agentic workflows are custom, so the most
> useful evals are usually the ones you write for the specific failures you
> found in your own error analysis.

> **In short.**
>
> - Development alternates between building and analyzing; most teams
>   under-invest in analysis.
> - The analysis grows with the system: read outputs, small evals, error
>   analysis, then component evals and larger held-out sets.

## Key takeaways

The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines:

- **Look first:** build a safe prototype and read outputs; failures tell you
  what to evaluate.
- **Measure the whole:** end-to-end evals graded by code where possible, by
  validated LLM judges otherwise, with error bars.
- **Find the cause:** read traces of failures and count which component is
  to blame.
- **Fix the part:** component evals to iterate fast, the cheapest fix first,
  then confirm end to end.
- **Then optimize:** cost and latency per step, after quality is good.

## Interview checkpoints

- **You built an agent and it is not good enough. What do you do first?** Run
  it on realistic inputs, read the outputs and traces, and note the recurring
  failures. Fix the obvious ones; build evals for the rest.
- **Describe the two axes of end-to-end evals, with an example in each
  quadrant.** Code vs. LLM judge, and per-example reference vs. shared
  criterion. Examples: extracted date vs. label (code, reference); length limit
  (code, shared); key points covered (judge, reference); chart rubric (judge,
  shared).
- **When would you use an LLM judge instead of code?** When the criterion
  requires understanding language, such as whether a point was made in
  different words, or tone. Use code for anything objective.
- **How do you know an LLM judge is reliable?** Compare it with human labels on
  a sample. Report agreement and Cohen's kappa, and re-check after changing the
  judge prompt or model.
- **What is a trace? What is a span?** A trace is the full record of one run
  through the system. A span is one step within it, such as an LLM call or a
  tool call, with its inputs, outputs, and timing.
- **Walk through error analysis.** Collect failed examples, step through each
  trace, mark the components whose output was clearly worse than an expert's
  given the same input, and count the share of failures per component.
- **Why don't the error-analysis percentages sum to 100%?** One failed example
  can have errors in more than one component.
- **The search step returned poor sources, and the selection step picked the
  best of them. Is selection at fault?** No. It did as well as possible with
  its input. The fault lies with search.
- **What is a component-level eval, and why use one?** It measures one
  component directly, for example retrieval precision and recall against
  expert-chosen sources. It is faster, cheaper, and less noisy than rerunning
  the whole system. Confirm the gains end to end.
- **Your eval has 20 examples, and a change moved accuracy from 80% to 85%.
  Did it help?** You cannot tell. The 95% interval at $n = 20$ is about ±17
  points. Look at paired differences on the same examples, add examples, and
  run repeated trials if outputs vary.
- **Your metric says no improvement, but you are sure the new version is
  better. What now?** Treat it as a problem with the eval. Inspect the
  examples, add cases that capture the difference, or change the grading.
- **What options do you have to improve an LLM component?** Better prompts and
  examples, a different model, decomposition or reflection, and fine-tuning as
  the last resort.
- **How do you reduce latency in an agentic workflow?** Time each step, then
  parallelize independent steps, use smaller or faster models where evals
  allow, choose faster providers, trim context, and stream the output.
- **When should you optimize cost?** After quality is acceptable. Measure the
  cost of each step and target the dominant ones with cheaper models, caching,
  batching, and fewer tokens.
